sources.finding: Workflow artifact attestations use the public-good instance for public repositories and GitHub's instance for private repositories. The guide describes separate bundle, artifact, CLI and trusted-root inputs, recommends refreshing roots when importing new signed material and warns an offline root file cannot reveal later key revocation. Its repository-certificate ID checks are not automatically the semantics of a release-service certificate.

The normal command covers both public-good and GitHub Sigstore instances. For a custom TUF mirror, --tuf-root must be a root.json securely obtained out-of-band. --verify-only checks the local TUF repository without emitting a trusted_root.jsonl. No displayed command is executed.

Release verification is documented separately: a cryptographically signed claim made by GitHub about a release and its assets. The command fetches that attestation and prints referenced asset digests. This fits the observed release-inventory predicate better than assuming a GitHub Actions workflow/build certificate. The manual does not itself authenticate the saved bundle or measure PDFium build materials.

The security model treats certificate identity, trusted verification material and transparency/time as separate verification concerns. It provides the custom-components and timestamp documentation leads followed in the next unit; a leaf-key match does not authenticate those inputs.

The default Cosign client starts from an embedded TUF root and obtains updated verification material from Sigstore's public-good root-signing repository. Fulcio and TSA entries require certificate-chain material, while Rekor/CT entries use public keys. Manually assembling a custom root is documented, not authority to select/install one here.

A historical version1 TUF root document is returned, not an issuer/TSA X509 chain. Discovery came from a third-party search snippet, not primary bootstrap authentication.
